items.en: The World of Meaning: The Body as Royal Court
items.zh: 通明觀 · 義世間 · 身內王法治正

zh: 第三、釋身內王法治正義。行者於三昧內願智之力，即復覺知身內，心為大王，上義下仁故，居在百重之內，出則有前後左右官屬侍衛。肺為司馬，肝為司徒，脾為司空，腎為大海，中有神龜，呼吸元氣，行風致雨，通氣四支。四支為民子，左為司命，右為司錄，主錄人命。齊中太一君亦人之主柱，天大將軍特進君王，主身內萬二千大神，太一有八使者，八卦是也，合為九卿。三焦關元為左社右稷，主姦賊。上焦通氣，入頭中為宗廟，王者於間治化。
en: Third, explaining the sense of the royal law of governance present within the body. The practitioner, through the power of samādhi and the wish-to-know, further becomes aware that, within the body, the mind serves as the Great King, exalting righteousness above and benevolence below, dwelling within a hundredfold enclosure, and, upon going forth, attended by officials and guards before, behind, to the left, and to the right. The lungs serve as the Minister of War; the liver as the Minister of the Masses; the spleen as the Minister of Works; and the kidneys as the great ocean, within which dwells the spirit-tortoise, breathing the primal energy, moving the wind and bringing the rain, circulating energy through the four limbs. The four limbs are the king's own subjects and children — the left serves as the Controller of Fate, and the right as the Controller of Records, governing the recording of human life.

Within the navel dwells the Lord of the Great Unity, also the very pillar upholding the person, the Great General of Heaven and Specially Advanced Sovereign King, governing the body's own twelve thousand great spirits. The Great Unity has eight envoys, these being precisely the eight trigrams, together forming the nine ministers. The triple burner and the pass at the origin serve as the altars of soil to the left and grain to the right, governing traitors and thieves. The upper burner, circulating energy, entering the head, forms the ancestral temple, where the king himself governs and transforms from within.

zh: 若心行正法，群下皆隨，則治正清夷，故五臟調和，六府通適，四大安樂，無諸疾惱，終保年壽。若心行非法，則群僚作亂，互相殘害，故四大不調，諸根暗塞，因此抱患致終，皆由行心惡法故。經言：「失魂即亂，失魄則狂，失意則惑，失志則忘，失神則死。當知外立王道治化，皆身內之法。」如是等義，具如《提謂經》說。
en: If the mind practices the correct dharma, the multitude below all follow accordingly, and governance is thereby correct and at peace — hence the five organs are harmonized, the six repositories function smoothly, the four elements are at ease, free of every affliction and trouble, and one's own years and life are thereby preserved to their fullest. But if the mind practices what is not the dharma, then the assembled officials fall into disorder, harming one another in turn — hence the four elements grow unregulated, the various faculties darken and become obstructed, and, because of this, illness is contracted and life comes to its end — all of this arising from the mind's own practice of unwholesome dharma. Hence the sūtra says: "Losing the cloud-soul brings disorder; losing the animal-soul brings madness; losing intention brings confusion; losing the will brings forgetfulness; and losing the spirit brings death. One should know that the royal way of governance established outwardly is, in every case, simply this same dharma present within the body itself." Such senses as these are all given in full within the Sūtra of Trapusa.

This political allegory of the body — mind as sovereign, organs as ministers of state, limbs as subjects, the whole apparatus of Han-dynasty bureaucratic cosmology (the Great Unity, the nine ministers, the altars of soil and grain) mapped directly onto physiology — completes the "world of meaning" the way the previous section's cosmology began it: the body is not only a small copy of the physical universe but a small copy of the political order as well. The closing moral is the section's real point and the reason it belongs in a meditation treatise at all: good governance and bodily health share a single cause, the mind's own practice of the correct dharma, so that self-cultivation and statecraft are, at bottom, the same discipline applied at different scales — a thoroughly Chinese framing of an originally Indian meditative insight.

items.en: The World of Meaning: The Body as Buddhadharma
items.zh: 通明觀 · 義世間 · 內世間義

zh: 第二、明內世間義相關者，上來所說，並與外義相關。所以者何？佛未出時，諸神仙世智等亦達此法，名義相對，故說前為外世間義也。是諸神仙雖復世智辯聰，能通達世間，若住此分別，終是心行理外，未見真實，於佛法不名聖人，猶是凡夫，輪迴三界二十五有，未出生死。若化眾生，名為舊醫，亦名世醫，故《涅槃經》云：「世醫所療治，差已還復發。若是如來療治者，差已不復發。」此如下說。今言內義世間者，即是如來出世，廣說一切教門名義之相，以化眾生。行者於定心內，意欲得知佛法教門主對之相，三昧、智慧、善根力故，即便覺知。
en: Second, clarifying how the internal world of meaning is interrelated: everything already discussed above is likewise interrelated with this external sense of meaning. Why is this? Before the Buddha appeared in the world, the various immortals and worldly sages had already penetrated this very dharma, matching its names and senses in just this way — hence what was given above is spoken of as the external world's own sense of meaning. Although these immortals possessed worldly wisdom, eloquence, and intelligence, able to penetrate the mundane world, should one remain fixed within this kind of discrimination, one's own mental conduct still, in the end, remains outside true principle, never yet having seen the truth — and, within the Buddhadharma, such a person is not named a sage at all, but remains, still, an ordinary person, turning through the three realms' twenty-five states of existence, never yet having left birth-and-death behind. Transforming sentient beings in this way is named the "old physician," also called the "worldly physician" — hence the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: "What the worldly physician treats, once cured, relapses once again. But what the Tathāgata himself treats, once cured, never relapses again." This will be discussed further below.

Here, what is spoken of as the internal world of meaning is precisely the Tathāgata's own appearance in the world, broadly expounding the mark of every teaching-gate's own name and sense, in order to transform sentient beings. The practitioner, within the concentrated mind, wishing to come to know the mark of how the Buddhadharma's own teaching-gates correspond to the body, through the power of samādhi, wisdom, and wholesome roots, thereupon becomes aware of this directly.

zh: 云何知如佛說五戒義為對五臟？已如前說，若四大、五陰、十二入、十八界、四諦、十二因緣悉人身內也。即知四大此義為對五臟：風對肝，火對心，水對腎，地對肺、脾。若聞五陰之名，尋即覺知對身五臟：色對肝，識對脾，想對心，受對腎，行對肺。名雖不次，而義相關。若聞十二入、十八界，亦復即知對內五臟。十入、十五界，義自可見。二入、三界，今當分別。五識悉為意入界，外五塵、內法塵以為法入界。此即二十三界相關。意識界者，初生五識為根，對外法塵即生意識，名意識界。
en: How does one know, as the Buddha teaches, that the sense of the five precepts corresponds to the five organs? This has already been given above: the four elements, the five aggregates, the twelve sense-bases, the eighteen elements, the Four Noble Truths, and the twelve links of dependent origination are, in every case, present within the body itself. One thereby knows that the sense of the four elements corresponds to the five organs in this way: wind corresponds to the liver; fire corresponds to the heart; water corresponds to the kidneys; and earth corresponds to the lungs and spleen.

Hearing the name of the five aggregates, one likewise becomes aware directly of their correspondence to the body's five organs: form corresponds to the liver; consciousness corresponds to the spleen; perception corresponds to the heart; sensation corresponds to the kidneys; and formation corresponds to the lungs. Though the names do not follow in the same sequence, their sense is nonetheless interrelated.

Hearing of the twelve sense-bases and the eighteen elements, one likewise knows their correspondence to the internal five organs directly — the ten sense-bases and fifteen elements' own sense may be seen for themselves; the remaining two sense-bases and three elements shall now be distinguished. The five sense-consciousnesses are, all together, the mind-base and mind-element; the external five sense-objects and the internal dharma-object together form the dharma-base and dharma-element. This accounts for the interrelation of these twenty-three elements. As for the mind-consciousness element: the five sense-consciousnesses first arise as its own faculty, and, in response to the external dharma-object, mind-consciousness thereupon arises — this is named the mind-consciousness element.

zh: 若聞五根，亦知對內五臟：憂根對肝，苦根對心，喜根對肺，樂根對腎，捨根對脾。五根因緣則具有三界。所以者何？憂根對欲界，苦根對初禪，喜根對二禪，樂根對三禪，捨根對四禪，乃至四空定皆名捨俱禪。當知三界亦為五臟，其義相關。聞說四生，亦覺知此義關五臟。所以者何？欲界具五根，五根關五臟，五臟關四大，四大對四生。一切卵生，多是風大性，身能輕舉故；一切濕生，多是水大性，因濕而生故；一切胎生，多屬地大性，其身重鈍故；一切化生，多屬火大性，火體無而欻有故，亦有光明故。
en: Hearing of the five faculties, one likewise knows their correspondence to the internal five organs: the faculty of sorrow corresponds to the liver; the faculty of suffering corresponds to the heart; the faculty of joy corresponds to the lungs; the faculty of happiness corresponds to the kidneys; and the faculty of equanimity corresponds to the spleen. Through the causes and conditions of these five faculties, the three realms, too, are thereby complete: the faculty of sorrow corresponds to the desire realm; the faculty of suffering corresponds to the first dhyāna; the faculty of joy corresponds to the second dhyāna; the faculty of happiness corresponds to the third dhyāna; and the faculty of equanimity corresponds to the fourth dhyāna, and, further still, all the way through the four formless concentrations, all of which are named the dhyāna joined with equanimity. One should know, then, that the three realms, too, correspond to the five organs, their sense mutually interrelated.

Hearing of the four kinds of birth, one likewise becomes aware that this sense, too, relates to the five organs. Why is this? The desire realm is complete with the five faculties; the five faculties relate to the five organs; the five organs relate to the four elements; and the four elements correspond to the four kinds of birth. Every kind of egg-birth is, for the most part, of the nature of the wind element, since the body is able to rise up lightly; every kind of moisture-birth is, for the most part, of the nature of the water element, since it arises through moisture; every kind of womb-birth belongs, for the most part, to the nature of the earth element, since its body is heavy and dull; and every kind of transformation-birth belongs, for the most part, to the nature of the fire element, since fire's own substance is absent and then suddenly present, and also possesses its own radiance.

zh: 如來為化三界四生故，說四諦、十二因緣、六波羅蜜，當知此三法藥神丹悉是對治眾生五臟、五根、陰故說。所以者何？如佛說一心四諦義，當知集諦對肝，因屬初生故；苦諦對心，果是成就故；道諦對肺，金能斷截故；滅諦對腎，冬藏之法，已有還無故。一心已對脾，開通四諦故。乃至十二因緣、六波羅蜜，類此可知也。此三種法藏，則廣攝如來一切教門，是故行者若心明利，諦觀身相，即便覺了一切佛法名義，故《華嚴經》言：「明了此身者，即是達一切。」是則說內義、世間義相關之相，意在幽微，非悟勿述。
en: The Tathāgata, in order to transform the three realms and the four kinds of birth, teaches the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the six pāramitās — one should know that these three dharma-medicines, this very spirit-elixir, are, in every case, taught precisely as an antidote for sentient beings' own five organs, five faculties, and aggregates.

Why is this? As the Buddha teaches the sense of the Four Noble Truths within a single mind, one should know: the truth of accumulation corresponds to the liver, since its cause belongs to what first arises; the truth of suffering corresponds to the heart, since its result is what comes to completion; the truth of the path corresponds to the lungs, since metal is able to sever and cut through; and the truth of cessation corresponds to the kidneys, the dharma of winter's own storing away, what once existed now returned to nothing. This single mind already corresponds to the spleen, since it opens up and penetrates all Four Noble Truths at once. And, further still, the twelve links of dependent origination and the six pāramitās may likewise be understood by this same pattern.

These three kinds of dharma-treasury thereby broadly encompass every one of the Tathāgata's own teaching-gates — hence the practitioner, should the mind be bright and sharp, closely contemplating the bodily mark, thereby comes to understand the name and sense of the whole Buddhadharma directly. Hence the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "One who clearly understands this very body has thereby penetrated everything whatsoever." This, then, explains the mark of how the internal world of meaning is interrelated with the world of meaning generally — its intent lies in the deeply hidden and subtle, not to be spoken of by anyone lacking realization.

This section makes an important move the previous cosmological one did not: it explicitly demotes the immortals' and worldly sages' own body-cosmos correspondence to something incomplete — real knowledge, but knowledge that "still, in the end, remains outside true principle" — before mapping the entire Buddhist doctrinal apparatus (aggregates, sense-bases, elements, faculties, the three realms, the four kinds of birth, and finally the Four Noble Truths themselves) onto the very same five organs. The worldly-physician-versus-Tathāgata simile makes the hierarchy explicit: correlative cosmology treats symptoms that recur, while the Buddhadharma, mapped onto the identical physiological substrate, treats the underlying cause. The Four Noble Truths' own placement is worth pausing on: accumulation (craving's cause) in the liver where new growth begins, suffering (the resulting fruit) in the heart, the path (which severs) in the lungs where metal's own cutting power resides, and cessation (a return to nothing) in the kidneys, associated with winter's own storing-away — each doctrinal category matched not arbitrarily but through the same five-phase logic already established for the cosmological correspondences.

items.en: Completing Initial Thought Within the World of Meaning
items.zh: 通明觀 · 義世間 · 釋成覺義
parent: The World of Meaning: The Body as Buddhadharma
通明觀 · 義世間 · 內世間義

zh: 第二、次釋成覺五支義者，亦為三義：一、下；二、次；三、上。今先釋覺支三義：一、下覺、大覺者，行者於靜心內悉覺上來所說內外二種世間之相，分別名義不同，即是隔別之相，故名覺義世。覺義世間，故名覺。大覺者，覺一切外名義雖別，而無實體，但依五臟，如因肝說不殺戒，歲星、太山、青帝、木魂、眼識、仁、毛、詩、角、性、震等諸法，此諸法不異肝，肝義不異不殺戒等，即是如，故名大覺。覺餘一切法如四臟亦如是。
en: Second, next explaining and completing the sense of initial thought and the five factors: this, too, has three senses — lower; middle; and upper.

Here, the three senses of the factor of initial thought are first explained. First, the lower initial thought and great initial thought: the practitioner, within the stilled mind, perceives fully the mark of these two kinds of world, internal and external, already given above, distinguishing their differing names and senses — this is precisely the mark of their own separation, hence this is named perceiving the world of meaning. Perceiving the world of meaning in this way, this is named initial thought.

As for great initial thought: perceiving that, although every external name and sense differs, none of them possesses any real substance of its own, all instead depending on the five organs — as, for instance, taking the liver as the basis for speaking of the precept against killing, Jupiter, Mount Tai, the Green Emperor, the wood-soul, eye-consciousness, benevolence, body-hair, the Book of Odes, the note jiao, its nature, thunder, and every other such dharma — none of these dharmas differs from the liver, and the liver's own sense does not differ from the precept against killing and the rest — this is precisely suchness, hence this is named great initial thought. Perceiving every other dharma as suchness, corresponding to the remaining four organs, follows this same pattern.

zh: 第二、次明覺、大覺者，行者覺知肝雖如不殺戒等一切法，而肝非肺、脾、心、腎等一切法，了知別異，名為覺。覺肝等諸法無常生滅，不異四臟等，諸法無常，名大覺。第三、次明上覺、大覺者，行者覺知肝等諸法八相別異，名為覺。覺此肝等諸法本來空寂，無有異相，名大覺。如此分別覺、大覺及世間、出世間相，雖與前同，而亦有異，深思自當可見。次釋思惟、大思惟者，觀於心性之義，類如前說。是則略明約義世諦中辯初禪覺支之相，餘觀、喜、安、定等，亦當如是一一分別。
en: Second, next clarifying initial thought and great initial thought: the practitioner, perceiving that although the liver is suchness with respect to the precept against killing and every other such dharma, the liver is nonetheless not the lungs, spleen, heart, kidneys, and every other such dharma, clearly understanding this distinction, this is named initial thought. Perceiving that the liver and the other organs' own dharmas are impermanent, arising and ceasing, no different from the impermanence of the remaining four organs and their own dharmas, this is named great initial thought.

Third, next clarifying the upper initial thought and great initial thought: the practitioner, perceiving that the liver and the other organs' own dharmas each bear the eight marks' own distinction, this is named initial thought. Perceiving that the liver and these other organs' own dharmas are originally empty and still, without any mark of difference at all, this is named great initial thought.

Distinguishing initial thought and great initial thought, and the mark of the mundane and the world-transcending, in this way, although the same as what was given before, nonetheless differs from it as well — examined deeply, this may be seen for oneself. Next, explaining deliberation and great deliberation, and the sense of contemplating the nature of mind, these follow the same pattern as already given before. This, in brief, clarifies, with reference to the conventional truth of the world of meaning, the mark of the first dhyāna's own factor of initial thought; the remaining factors of sustained reflection, joy, ease, and concentration should likewise each, in turn, be distinguished in this same way.

The same lower/middle/upper, three-grade structure already used for the root world is applied again here, but now the object of contemplation has shifted entirely — from the body's own physical constituents to the vast web of correlations just established (an organ, its associated planet, virtue, note, and classic text, all recognized as "suchness" with one another). The logic, though, is identical throughout this whole fascicle: multiplicity distinguished, then multiplicity recognized as sharing one nature, then even that shared nature seen as empty. This closes the world of meaning's own treatment of the first dhyāna for a practitioner of middle faculty.

quiz.q: In the royal law within the body, what offices do the mind and organs hold?
options: mind as Great King; lungs, liver, spleen as ministers; kidneys as the ocean with a spirit-tortoise
quiz.why: The mind is the Great King; the lungs are Minister of War, liver Minister of the Masses, spleen Minister of Works; the kidneys are the great ocean with a spirit-tortoise.

quiz.q: What happens to the body when the mind practices the correct dharma or not?
options: correct: harmony and long life; incorrect: disorder, illness, and death
quiz.why: If the mind practices the correct dharma, all follow, the organs harmonize, and life is preserved; if not, the officials rebel, the elements fall out of balance, and illness leads to death.

quiz.q: According to the sūtra, what results from losing each of the five spirits?
options: losing the cloud-soul: disorder; animal-soul: madness; intention: confusion; will: forgetfulness; spirit: death
quiz.why: Losing the cloud-soul brings disorder, the animal-soul madness, intention confusion, the will forgetfulness, and the spirit death.

quiz.q: In which sūtra are these senses of royal law given in full?
quiz.why: Such senses are all given in full in the Sūtra of Trapusa, as §9 also says.

quiz.q: Why is the preceding called the "external" world of meaning, and how are the immortals who knew it regarded?
options: immortals knew it before the Buddha; still outside principle, they are ordinary people, "old" or "worldly physicians"
quiz.why: Immortals and worldly sages knew this before the Buddha; remaining within such discrimination, they stay outside true principle, are not sages, and as teachers are "old" or "worldly physicians."

quiz.q: How does the Nirvāṇa Sūtra compare worldly physicians with the Tathāgata?
options: worldly cures relapse; the Tathāgata's do not
quiz.why: What the worldly physician cures relapses; what the Tathāgata cures never relapses.

quiz.q: Which matching of the elements and aggregates to the organs is correct?
options: wind–liver, fire–heart, water–kidneys, earth–lungs and spleen; form–liver, consciousness–spleen, perception–heart, sensation–kidneys, formation–lungs
quiz.why: Wind corresponds to the liver, fire the heart, water the kidneys, earth the lungs and spleen; form to the liver, consciousness the spleen, perception the heart, sensation the kidneys, formation the lungs.

quiz.q: How do the five faculties correspond to the three realms?
options: sorrow: desire realm; suffering: first dhyāna; joy: second; happiness: third; equanimity: fourth and the formless
quiz.why: Sorrow corresponds to the desire realm, suffering to the first dhyāna, joy to the second, happiness to the third, and equanimity to the fourth and the formless concentrations.

quiz.q: Which relation of the four kinds of birth to the elements is correct?
options: egg: wind; moisture: water; womb: earth; transformation: fire
quiz.why: Egg-birth is mostly wind (the body rises lightly), moisture-birth water, womb-birth earth (heavy and dull), transformation-birth fire (suddenly present, with radiance).

quiz.q: Which matching of the Four Truths in one mind to the organs is correct?
options: accumulation–liver, suffering–heart, path–lungs, cessation–kidneys, the one mind–spleen
quiz.why: Accumulation corresponds to the liver, suffering to the heart, the path to the lungs (metal cuts), cessation to the kidneys (winter storage), and the one mind to the spleen.

quiz.q: Which Avataṃsaka line is cited for understanding all Buddhadharma by contemplating the body?
options: One who clearly understands this body has penetrated everything
quiz.why: The Avataṃsaka says one who clearly understands this body has penetrated everything; the point is subtle and not to be spoken without realization.

quiz.q: In the lower grade of the world of meaning, how is great initial thought illustrated with the liver?
options: external names differ but depend on the organs; the liver and all its correlates are not different—suchness
quiz.why: External names differ but lack substance, resting on the organs; the liver and its correlates such as the precept against killing, Jupiter, and Mount Tai do not differ, which is suchness. C and D are the middle and upper grades.
